en: Composed by the Tang Dynasty Tiantai monk Zhìràn.
Regarding the passage "neither aware nor knowing," the following four lines are explained in relation to the Four Noble Truths.
However, at the outset, the text should have listed all four lines; it is merely abbreviated here. This section consists of three parts: first, [the introduction].
First, an explanation based on ordinary beings; second, an explanation based on the stages; third, an explanation based on the three periods of time.
The first section further consists of three parts:
the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.
Regarding the initial passage: the section beginning with "utterly does not speak" indicates *duḥkha* (suffering).
"Fire" refers to the three realms, the five turbidities, and the eight sufferings.
The section beginning with "not understanding fire" indicates *samudaya* (the origin), for fire is inherently capable of burning, just as the origin of suffering invites suffering.
The phrase "already not knowing" below marks the loss of the Path; because one does not fear injury, it is said that one is "not startled," and "injury" here means loss.
The phrase "not considering severance" below marks the loss of extinction; since there is no body of the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya), the life-force of wisdom is also severed.
The passage beginning with "sentient beings" explains the preceding four lines. Since the aggregates (*skandhas*) are necessarily suffering, this explains the preceding phrase "there is suffering";

because they are entirely unaware [of this], they do not recognize suffering. The section beginning with "not knowing" explains the preceding "accumulation" (*samudaya*). The phrases "four inversions" and "three poisons" explain the preceding "there is accumulation"; because they are entirely ignorant [of this], they do not recognize accumulation.
The three poisons are afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), while the four inversions are afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*).
The phrase "Since they do not... below explains the loss of the path and cessation; because one does not know suffering and its origin, both the path and cessation are lost.
"Being ignorant of delusion" means being ignorant of the origin [of suffering]; since one is ignorant of the origin, one does not feel anxiety regarding suffering.
"Delusion invading the Dharma-body" means losing the Truth of the Path; it inevitably damages the life of wisdom and results in losing the Truth of Cessation.
The section beginning with "In this way" concludes [the preceding].

Regarding the subsequent section beginning with "Because of not hearing," which explains by assigning stages, first two pairs of lines provide a positive explanation, followed by the final two lines providing a negative explanation.

In the initial passage, the first two phrases correspond to hearing and reflection; it should have stated, "not awakening through hearing and reflection," and "not knowing wisdom through cultivation," but the text is abbreviated.
The subsequent two phrases then advance to the stage of the sages.

Next, regarding the counter-explanation (*pratiṣedha-vyākhyāna*): it should be stated that one does not startle because there is no vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), and one does not fear because there is no conceptualization (*manasikāra*). Since the text provides a counter-explanation, it says, "One startles and awakens because of the vision of the truths," and so forth.
This clarifies that the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths has been perfected, such that the two delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*) are ultimately exhausted.

Because these delusions are exhausted, the Four Truths are fully revealed; for the first time, one attains the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), and the distinction between delusion and awakening is initially made. This is like someone who has long been lost suddenly finding the right path, hence the term "startled awakening"; furthermore, through renewed revulsion and dread, the path of delusion is finally brought to an end.

Next, regarding the three periods of time: it is not said that one contemplates the past or its origination because one directly observes present suffering through present origination, and also observes present suffering through past origination—just as it is called "saṃsāra" within the context of causes and conditions. Although the three periods are discussed, one correctly observes present suffering in order to sever present origination; once present origination is severed, suffering will now cease. Therefore, we know that failing to perceive present suffering constitutes a delusion regarding both suffering and its origination, which is able to summon future suffering. Since one is deluded regarding suffering and origination, there can logically be no path or cessation. Thus, the sufferings of two periods are cited to encompass all three; as in the cited text, this is simply using suffering to encompass origination.

However, although these three preceding explanations differ in their focus—whether on ordinary beings, specific stages, and so forth—in general, they all concern delusion regarding the truths; because of this delusion regarding the truths, the eight types of suffering oppress the body.
Regarding the phrase "the five consciousnesses" and so forth: "逼" (bi) means "proximate.
When turbidity resides within the five consciousnesses, it is termed "proximate"; because it directly impinges upon oneself, it is called "逼身" (bi shēn), meaning "impinging upon the body."

At the same time, the mental consciousness experiences the objects of suffering together with them; this is not the case during the first moment before discrimination has arisen, and furthermore, it is because the substance of these five consciousnesses themselves is the retributive [consciousness] and the eight types of suffering.
How could that which is proximate exceed this? Therefore, how could it simultaneously give rise to weariness and aversion?

Consequently, this mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) cannot, by means of this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), form a meditative contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); they can only perform discrimination to constitute the three feelings (*vedanā*). Because the meaning of these three feelings is established, it is said to "touch one's person" (*ch'i-chi*); because it is extremely pressing, it is called "urgent" (*ch'e*).

Therefore, each and every suffering arises first through the five consciousnesses as they encounter their respective objects, and subsequently reaches the sixth consciousness for further discrimination; since the causes of suffering are thus established, how could one possibly develop revulsion?

It is also said [in another commentary]: In the past, the Mahāyāna was termed "the seed" (*bīja*); merit (*guṇa*) is precisely the wisdom belonging to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Taking this very wisdom as its essence, it is oppressed by suffering; when the Great Principle and the Wisdom Vehicle both encounter the accumulation of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*), being neither aware nor cognizant of it is called "being oppressed by fire."

Regarding the passage beginning with "Now it is said," this refers solely to the names of the defilements (*kaṣāya*) and need not be correlated with the Great [Vehicle]. Since sentient beings have already been wandering in saṃsāra and do not even know themselves as small, all these meanings are combined to constitute the five defilements (*pañca-kaṣāyāḥ*).

Regarding the statement that the four factors beginning with "non-awakening" constitute the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kāṣāya*): these four phrases are simply delusions regarding the Four Noble Truths; because of this delusion regarding the truths, sentient beings themselves become defiled.
Next, "the coming of fire" and so forth refer to the defilement of life (*āyus-kāṣāya*); because suffering is intense and lifespan is shortened, life becomes defiled.

"The mind does not feel weary" and so forth refer to the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kāṣāya*); because one does not grow weary of suffering and constantly remains within the three realms, one inevitably encounters the three minor [calamities], which is termed the defilement of the eon.
The phrase "and so forth" intends to criticize the former masters, asserting that it is unnecessary to interpret this in relation to the Great [Fire].
Because of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), it is precisely appropriate to expand upon the fire previously seen; therefore, the preceding section merely states, "arising from the four sides."

Regarding the passage beginning with "The elder acted thus," first the hands and body of the donor are explained, and next the garment and bowl (or lap-cloth) that are given are explained; since both the agent and the object are negated, it is said that "[he] does not obtain [it]."

The initial text consists of ten sections: first, the heading; second, the citation and application of the analogy; third, from "relying on samādhi" onwards, the clarification of the basis for the two meanings; fourth, from "wisdom and severance" onwards, the clarification of the functions of the two meanings; fifth, from "this" onwards, the clarification of the gates of the two meanings; sixth, from "exhorting one to immediately" onwards, the explanation by means of the four *siddhāntas*; seventh, from "the Tathāgata" onwards, the clarification of the intent behind employing the two meanings; eighth, from "therefore we know" onwards, the conclusion and return to the source; ninth, from "therefore the preceding text" onwards, the citation of evidence; tenth, from "the previous praise" onwards, the re-indication of the preceding evidence.
The first four [points] can be understood as before.

Regarding the fifth, "This" and so forth: by correlating cause and effect, it is exhorted that this is the gate for those who cultivate wisdom (*jñāna*), and cautioned that this is the gate for those who practice abandonment (*prahāṇa*); therefore, it is said that one enters through these two gates.

Now, regarding the fact that admonitions are mentioned again within the context of the "Gate of Exhortation," it is because the essential nature of these gates logically requires mutual inclusion; they are explained separately for the sake of convenience in expressing their respective meanings.

Among the six types of *siddhānta*, it is said that "these two *siddhāntas* serve as skillful means (*upāya*) for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). These two *siddhāntas* constitute the wisdom and cessation attained through cultivation, whereas the ultimate truth is the Dharmakāya of innate virtue. At the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, it was stated that the Dharmakāya cannot grasp objects by means of wisdom and cessation; therefore, the Buddha ceased his transformative activity.
Question: Why does it not say that the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint) each has two gates that differ according to individual inclinations?
Furthermore, we have heard that both types of joy are worldly.

Therefore, this Buddha-vehicle generates goodness and extinguishes evil by universally arising through the eight gates; within the four gates of the Perfect and Distinct [teachings], there are two and four respectively for each. Thus, these two gates encompass all dharmas. The rest is as stated in the text.
Regarding the explanation of the "bestowal" (*pradāna*), the text is further divided into three parts:

first, the presentation of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*) as the basis; second, the presentation of previous interpretations; and third, the formal explanation beginning with the words "Now, we take... (*idānīm gṛhṇīmaḥ*).
Although the initial [section] relies upon the Tripiṭaka, it merely analyzes the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) without clarifying the dharma-gates (*dharmamukha*).
Regarding the subsequent "Ancient Exegesis," the first master asks: "Why would it be unreasonable for this to be the cause and fruit of the Mahāyāna?"
However, because it lacks the characteristics of transformative teaching (*śāsanā*), we do not employ it.

Furthermore, since the previous master stated that this was extracted from the *Āgama* scriptures, one should not use a small [vehicle] to explain a great [one]; even if it were called Mahāyāna, how would it differ from the Four Stages?
As for those who speak of the "gài" (a fold or pocket), it refers to the hem or sleeve of a garment;
such usage is not employed nowadays.
Would one use a sleeve meant for extinguishing a fire to carry a child?

Next, within the section on "Correct Understanding," the phrase "also taking" below serves as the application of the analogy; the Buddha himself explains the meaning here—how could it be the same as worldly sentiment?
This section is divided into five parts:
first, citing the subsequent passage.
Next, from "Supernatural Power" (*ṛddhi*) downward is the formal explanation: the body and hands refer back to the previous explanation of the robe-pouch and so forth;
third, from "Tathāgata" downward clarifies the threefold intention of its use;
fourth, from "Robe-pouch" downward clarifies the intention behind establishing the name.
The first three [phrases] are easy to understand.

Regarding the statement "the names are concise while the meanings are profound": the two aspects of knowledge (*jñāna*) and vision (*darśana*) constitute the conciseness of the names, and because they encompass all phenomena (*dharma*), the meanings are profound.
This is like a garment-bag: it is "concise" because it has only one opening, yet it is "profound" because it contains much.

Regarding the "Four Fearlessnesses" (*catur-vaiśāradya*), a brief account may be found in the *Dharmadhātu-krama* and the seventh fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* provides an extensive explanation. Generally speaking, "fearlessness" means that because one is inwardly filled with the Ten Powers (*daśa-bala*), there is no timidity in outward application; this is termed fearlessness.
The Buddha himself spoke these sincere words:

"I am the all-knowing one and the all-seeing one. There is not a single śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, nor a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or any other being, who can say that the Tathāgata does not know, even down to the slightest trace of fear."

Regarding "employing [the teachings] in relation to the Four Truths": the path that exhausts suffering is the Truth of Suffering; the explanation of what obstructs the path is the Truth of Origination; all-encompassing wisdom is the Truth of the Path; and the exhaustion of outflows is the Truth of Cessation. These four sets of Four Truths constitute the Four Kinds of Fearlessness. Now, they must reside in the Perfect [Teaching], pervading all four while remaining free from duality to form the fourfold set. Since both rely upon the Truths, and the Truths serve as their basis, it is called "Peaceful Stability" (An).

Regarding the term "power" (*bala*) used generally among the ten powers (*daśabala*): the internal, actualized wisdom and cognition attained by all Buddhas is perfectly clear and distinct; because nothing can surpass it and nothing can destroy it, it is called "power."

Because the distinction between the internal and external aspects of the fearlessnesses and powers encompasses each [category] exhaustively, they are termed "horizontal"; because the ten powers rely upon principle, they are termed "vertical.
Thus, how could the clarification of the truths across these ten points not be profoundly settled?

Although fearlessness and powers (bala) may be categorized as internal or external, they are now fully possessed both internally and externally because they are considered here in terms of their function.
Fifth, from "the three sevens" onwards, the intention behind the transformative teaching is summarized.
Regarding the statement "yet sentient beings cannot endure it," this refers to the "Great [Vehicle] Bestowal" (*mahā-dāna*); the term "cannot endure" is used here as a figurative expression.

From "there is only one gate" up to "narrow and small," there are two parts: first, pointing out the similarity to the preceding category; second, providing a detailed explanation by dividing the gates.

Regarding the initial statement, "The meaning is as explained above," this refers to the gateway of the vehicle mentioned above; here, too, it is the gateway of the vehicle of the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).
If one has already exited the gate of the house but has not yet entered the gateway of the vehicle, it is called "narrow and small" because it is difficult to traverse.
The initial statement "individually" refers to the analysis of the characters by dividing them according to three distinct meanings.
Within this, the first part provides the direct explanation, while the section beginning with "teaching and principle" explains the underlying reasons.

Regarding the initial formal explanation: since "one" (the individual) refers to principle and "gate" (the teaching) pertains to doctrine, the "small" refers to a lack of spiritual capacity; because there is no practice, one does not enter into either principle or doctrine, and is therefore termed "narrow and small."

Regarding the statement, "It does not admit of annihilationism, eternalism, or the seven expedient means," one should say "annihilationism, eternalism, and the seven expedient means"; since these do not enter into reality, they are said figuratively to be "not admitted."
To say that "sentient beings cannot understand this principle through their own teachings" means they merely adhere to expedient practices.

As for "universal explanation," it refers to the three—principle, teaching, and practice—each of which clarifies a single gate as being narrow and limited; because one does not enter [the path], one cannot attain the fruit.

First, regarding the perspective of principle (*li*): because there is only the single *dharmadhātu*, it is said to be "unmixed. Because this single principle universally pervades all things, it is said to be "capable of penetrating" insofar as it enables one to reach this principle. Because sentient beings (the "sons") do not enter [this principle], it is said to be "difficult to know."

Regarding the provisional teaching (*yàojiào*), it refers exclusively to the application of the perfect principle (*yuánlǐ*) to the teachings, clarifying that "entering" and "exiting" are merely matters of principle and teaching.

When it says, "Ordinary people do not know how to exit," it means they have not yet reached the point where the two vehicles (*èshèng*) have already exited through the gate of the house via the Lesser Teaching (*xiǎojiào*).
"Does not know how to enter" means not knowing the gate of the vehicle; since the two teachings for the two vehicles only lead out through the gate, it is said they "know little.
Because the former teaching did not fully elucidate [the truth], they "perpetually do not know how to enter."
Regarding the phrase, “Although a bodhisattva knows for himself that he has emerged,” this applies generally to all bodhisattvas.
For although a bodhisattva of the Tripiṭaka [teaching] may have emerged from the formal teachings, he has not yet emerged from the three great eons and one hundred kalpas.
Furthermore, regarding the bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching who possess dull faculties, they are the same as the two vehicles in that they do not yet know the point of entry; hence the word "also.

As for "stripping away the seven expedient means": previously, when they were granted [the teaching], it was said they knew the exit, yet because they had not yet entered the reality, it was called not knowing the entry. If one speaks in terms of stripping them away, they do not even know the exit.
Why is this? Because they do not know their own superior, middling, or inferior natures, they do not know how to emerge.

Speaking in general terms, one might still understand how to enter through the universal and particular *vaipulya* gates; however, because these involve the path of provisional teaching (*śāsana-mārga*), when speaking from the perspective of negation, those in the stages prior to the [first] ground of the distinct teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna-śikṣā*) all remain ignorant. Since they do not even know their own superior, middling, or inferior natures, how much less could they know the rain of the single ground?

Because it is said that those who do not know the provisional side do not know anything at all, the stage prior to the grounds in the Separate Teaching (biejiao), although they know the Middle Way, still relies on the provisional path. According to the teaching path, this continues until one enters the [first] ground; however, since upon entering the ground one must necessarily realize [the truth], the provisional is set aside and no longer discussed.
The section beginning with "As stated above" is an introduction of scriptural citations.
This is because those at the seven stages of expedient means (saptavidha-upāya) have not yet entered the Buddha-vehicle (buddhayāna).

Regarding the phrase "cannot by means of the teaching," etc.: the term "expedient means" necessarily implies a penetration toward the ultimate reality; if the Buddha has not yet opened [this door], they cannot, by means of their own teaching, penetrate to the ultimate.

Regarding the phrase "about to discuss": previously, before the [defilements] were rejected, it was not said that there was no capacity [for awakening]; rather, because they were briefly opened up prior to being explained, it is called "about to discuss. This can be understood by reference to their practice.

Regarding the phrase "childish and ignorant": if the former masters claim that the wholesome states of humans and devas constitute childishness, this would mean that great goodness has not yet arisen; how then could these be called childish?
The present [explanation] is correct.

Regarding the phrase "clinging with attachment" and so forth: previously it was explained that because the wholesome is weak, there is as yet no conscious awareness; now it is explained that because the unwholesome is powerful, one plays and is thereby consumed by fire.
"The time of cause" refers to the initial stage of regressing from the Great Vehicle.
"The time of fruit" refers to the stage of undergoing the eight sufferings.
After having regressed from the Great Vehicle, one clings to the causes of craving and views; the environment and its inhabitants are precisely the fruits of craving and views.
Because attachment to the desire realm is the basis and attachment to the higher realms is the actual [object], it is said that "dhyāna-concentration" and so forth [are the antidotes].

Regarding the section from "the characteristics of the antidote" to "the Lesser Vehicle": here, what is called the "antidote" in the Mahāyāna gate of admonition is not the same as the impermanence and so forth of the Lesser Vehicle; therefore, it cites the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and other practices from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as all belonging to the Mahāyāna. In contemplating impurity and so forth, both subject and object are forgotten and are both unobtainable.
Question:
If that is so, it is merely the contemplation of principle; why is it called an "antidote" (pratipakṣa)?
Answer:
When practicing the counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*), both subject and object are empty; this case is likewise so.

By means of great transformation through giving, it further causes one to leave behind turbidity; for the Buddha, this is precisely the characteristic of the Mahāyāna. Therefore, it is named the "counteractive characteristic of the Great Vehicle."
Regarding the phrase "once [the afflictions] have arisen," this refers to what is remedied by the Great [Vehicle]; for one ought to employ the Great to abandon evil.

As for the passage beginning with "if for a long time," it means that if one dwells [in delusion] for a long time, both the Small and the Great will be lost through the views and thoughts [of affliction].

Regarding the passage from "without alarm" to "as above," this refers to the extensive explanation provided above concerning the text on "non-awakening" and so forth, which applies to ordinary beings and the three periods of time.

Regarding "turning one's back to the light" and so forth, east and west are metaphors for suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*); if one clearly perceives suffering and its origin, one is facing toward the light.
Because one does not know suffering, the origin [of suffering] arises, like the sun moving from east to west;
because one does not recognize the origin, suffering is summoned, like the sun racing from west to east.
The meaning of "rushing" (*chi-zǒu*) is one and the same; thus, the Sūtra refers to it as "playful sport" (*xì*).

Death is like going away, and birth is like returning; having returned, one goes away again. Thus, the cycle of birth and death is unceasing. Unlike the lifespan in those two transformed lands (*biàn-yì èr tǔ*), this [existence] is as swift as a rapid rush.

Furthermore, arising from suffering and proceeding toward its accumulation is like going; arising from accumulation and returning to suffering is like coming back. One suffering and one accumulation, one birth and one death—therefore, this is called "running to and fro."
Regarding the phrase "Although one employs the great [vehicle] as a model," etc.: it means that although one hears [the teaching], one does not accept it, regarding it merely as seeing one's father.
Just as one might see one's father and flee in fear, thereby losing the benefit of both hearing and seeing; thus it is said, "merely."
"Already" (*yi*) means "ceased.
Furthermore, because the stimulus strikes the response, it is called "viewing"; yet because the stimulus arises without being received, it is said to be "already [ceased].

From "Mahāyāna" down to "the father's life is severed," the Mahāyāna is treated as both father and son’s life-force. Although one may provide great salvation, if the seed has not yet been attained, it must not be allowed to perish; therefore, even if one wishes to employ the minor vehicle (*hīnayāna*), it is for the sake of preserving the great life-force so that the merit of transformation is not abandoned.

Regarding the phrase "what was previously said touches one's own person": when one first regresses from the Mahāyāna, it coincides with the arising of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). At this initial stage, although the great goodness is still present within one, if one does not emerge from it after a long time and continues to transmigrate through the five turbidities, one will surely be consumed by them; thus, both the Great and the Small Vehicles are lost.

These words are spoken briefly for the sake of the occasion; thus it is said that if one does not emerge at this time, the Mahāyāna roots of goodness are in fact never severed. The intent is to urge one to emerge quickly by pressing upon the inevitability of death.
If one does not emerge for a long time, it is equivalent in meaning to death; therefore, it is said that this carries the sense of "death.

Regarding the intent of the questions from the passage "In the case of what is being burned" up to "if one does not emerge in time," etc.: the former [passage] concerns the distinction between emerging and being consumed by fire together, while the latter concerns the distinction between the internal and external. Since these two passages appear contradictory, how should their meanings be understood?

Next, regarding the meaning of the response beginning with "The previous attainment": the dharmas should not be identical, as the two meanings are distinct; from both the perspective of the text and the underlying principle, the two intentions differ.
If we follow the preceding text, since that text is based on the Hīnayāna, it emerges from the gate of being "burned" according to the Lesser Teaching;

thus, for the time being, it refers to the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcāṅga-dharmakāya*). If the meaning encompasses both [the teaching and the principle], then the Dharma extends to two kinds. If the Dharma and its response are contrasted, the principle must be the eternally abiding Dharma-body, which has already emerged. However, in this treatise, as we discuss the responsive body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and sentient beings receiving transformation, both the capacity of the beings and the response are saved; therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] "emerges at the proper time."

If they do not accept transformation, their spiritual capacity will cease and my response will fade; as for the meaning of entering extinction through the severance of the ashes, it is appropriate that both be consumed by fire. Because they are consumed, it is fitting that the lives of both son and father should end; using this as a suitable analogy, I urge them on with urgency.
Question:
It was stated previously that those who attain this Dharma-body have neither the Great nor the Small Dharmas burned away; why, then, is it necessary to speak of "exiting"?
Answer:

It is simply because there is no burning that it is called "emerging. If this is so, then all phenomena (dharmas) should likewise be without burning; they should fundamentally be identical to things, such that one speaks of them as "burning" in accordance with those things. From the perspective of principle (li), phenomena should be indestructible; yet from the perspective of phenomena (shi), when a thing burns, the Buddha emerges.
The present explanation that both are burned together means they emerge at the same time; therefore, it says "if they are not equal.
Some say: "The response and the stimulus occur simultaneously."

Now, it is said that while one has grasped the principle of emerging together, one has lost the meaning of being burned together; therefore, the necessity of being burned together is used to ensure they emerge simultaneously.

From the passage "Knowing the child's previous [nature]" onwards, it clarifies that because there are those with small capacities, he provides a small teaching to connect with them; because he opens the One into three, it is called "separate."
Regarding the passage from "Furthermore, he knows" to "slightly strong": it is weak because of a great regression.
There are two meanings for "slightly strong":
first, the weariness with suffering; second, the application of the remedy.

Regarding the phrase "retrogression from the sixth mind," according to the intent of the *Ratnakaranda-śrāvakabhūmi-sūtra* (or *Yingluo jing*), Śāriputra retrogressed from the sixth mind within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). This likely means that prior to this point he had severed both the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) and those of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), yet by the time he reached the sixth mind, his realization regarding the afflictions of views was still not exhaustive, and thus he was still subject to retrogression at that stage.
Regarding the "Praise of the Three Chariots," someone asks:

Why are there three chariots, two messengers, and one city; why is there a city but no chariot [in the latter case]; and since both are metaphors for skillful means (*upāya*), why do their numbers differ?
He has already answered that there is more to be said; now he answers further.

Generally, when establishing analogies, each is presented from a particular perspective; one must not cling to a single view and thereby doubt other paths. Thus, the numbers one, two, and three are merely matters of separation and combination, distinguished only to correspond to the differences among the three stages of faith and understanding. Therefore, they are distinct only in this way; all serve as analogies for the skillful means (*upāya*), and their underlying meaning does not differ.

The chariot is threefold because it generally encompasses all skillful means; the messengers are twofold because they are distinguished according to their difficulties; the city is one because it is the destination of both [the chariot and the messengers]; yet one should know that the city is also twofold because it follows the people [who enter it]. Thus, it is said that two are spoken of regarding the place of rest. The chariot is also twofold because it follows the difficulties. Furthermore, the messengers also include Bodhisattvas by implication; these three all possess the principles of persons, teachings, practices, and realizations.

If one speaks of the city as a transformation, it is likewise non-existent; the chariot exists because it relies upon construction; the messenger exists because he is identical [to his function] by way of provisional designation; yet because the provisional is not real, he is also non-existent. When the provisional and the real are contrasted, both are compatible with the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).

From the perspective of provisional transformation, both exist; from the perspective of ultimate reality, both are non-existent. Because both are encompassed by the provisional and the real, there is both existence and non-existence; because they are equally based on a single principle, both are negated.

Regarding "Exhortation and Demonstration": it should be shown that [the section on] exhortation comes first; following the sequence of the sutra, one first exhorts and subsequently demonstrates, which would likewise be without fault.

Within the section on realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), the phrase "bestowing" (*dadāti*) means that one is already correctly established in realization oneself, and because one also causes others to realize it, it is called "bestowing."
Regarding the statement "the previous verse was originally concise," this refers, for example, to the original text simply stating, "This is called turning the wheel of Dharma," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "extensively clarifying" up to "six phrases," the four [categories] such as the noble ones (*ārya*) are combined into four, while those of vision (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) constitute two.

The reason why these factors are grouped together by the Wise is as follows: the four foundations of mindfulness are one because they share the same dharma; "Heat" and "Summit" are one because they both involve falling back; "Patience" is one because there is no longer emerging from contemplation; the "Supreme Worldly Dharmas" are one because they are unsurpassed; and the paths of seeing and cultivation are each one because they differ from one another.
This has been explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Noble Ones" (*Āryapudgala-nirdeśa*) of the *Abhidharmakośa*; here it shall be briefly clarified.

Regarding the "thirty-two truths," there are sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) for each of the upper and lower [realms]; since these are discussed together, they total thirty-two, as briefly explained in the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Shiqian*.

Regarding the phrase "not distinct from the receptivity to the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*): the mind of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) shares the same moment as this [receptivity], entering into the receptivity to suffering and observing the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) simultaneously. One should say that among the four [truths], it observes one aspect; however, because it is identical to the receptivity to suffering, it is mentioned collectively.
Regarding the phrase "running forth to see the fifteen moments of the Path of Seeing," the sixteen moments following the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) are all untainted (*anāsrava*).
Some say that these sixteen moments still belong to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The categories differ.
The phrase "there is then the sound of nirvana" refers to the first turning of the wheel.

Regarding the practice of Mahayana contemplation within the mind: generally, when one relies on the text to perform contemplation, it mostly pertains to the Perfect Teaching (Yuan), so that each and every passage does not contradict what one has studied; this is because one is not merely enumerating the teachings of others.

Regarding "the initial arrival at 'aspiration'": when the mind looks toward the object of contemplation, it is termed "aspiration"; however, because the mind has not yet accorded with the object, it is not yet "fulfilling the aspiration.
Regarding "the object" up to "courage": when the objects are many and contemplation is few, one is not a person of courageous progress.

"Refining the mind by means of the object" means that one again uses the mind to contemplate the wondrous object and thereby refines the mind; by repeatedly performing this contemplation of the mind, it becomes sharp.
"Mutually refining the mind and the object" means that previously one used the object to refine the mind, and earlier one used the mind to contemplate the object; therefore, they are called "mutual."

Regarding the phrase "the mind-king" and so forth: when first applying the mind to cultivate contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), there is nothing that does not begin with the sixth consciousness as the king to initiate the contemplation. Even if the object of contemplation becomes perfectly integrated and non-dual, since coarse afflictions have not yet been eliminated, it still remains within the domain of the sixth consciousness as its king. This continues until the six sense faculties are purified; as long as one has not transcended them, one has not left the realm of the "king. This is because it is the sovereign number of the *darśana-heya* (afflictions abandoned through insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (afflictions abandoned through cultivation).

If one wishes to explain this according to the classification of teachings (*yàojiào*), there are four distinct sets of stages for the worthies and sages (*xiánshèng*) that differ in their progression;

here, we are currently in the Tripitaka (*sānzàng*). Regarding the phrase "In the preceding explanation of the Dharma, it was first clarified," etc.: in the *Shìjiā* (Śākya) chapter, there are six lines of verse within the section revealing the ultimate truth (*xiǎnshí*). First, the explanation based on the "Fourfold Identity" (*sìyī*) constitutes the literal interpretation of the text; next, the explanation based on "Seeking the Chariot" constitutes the basis of the parable. Specifically, the first two lines—beginning with "I see my sons, the disciples of the Buddha"—refer to the three types of bodhisattvas who heard the various provisional teachings mentioned previously.
Next, the two lines and one phrase beginning with "Then I immediately had this thought" clarify the Buddha’s joy when obstacles are removed.
The statement "Now I rejoice and am fearless" means that he rejoices precisely because the obstacles have been removed.

Regarding the statement, "Now, first the avoidance of calamity is clarified, and later the seeking of the vehicle is clarified," since the preceding and succeeding sections differ, Guangzhai directly equates the great capacity with the avoidance of calamity; therefore, [the author] refutes him.
This clarifies that the differences between the earlier and later parts of the sutra text do not imply that the removal of hindrances occurs sequentially;
rather, it is because all the śrāvakas had first removed their defilements, and now their great capacities have been awakened.

Regarding the phrase "if [they] are fully endowed," etc., by means of the textual sequence of the Dharma and the analogy, the difficulties are avoided through the prior and posterior interchanges of the capacity [of the recipient]. Based on these differences, the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are explained; first, two propositions are explained, while the remaining two are referred back to what precedes.

Regarding these two phrases: because the previous two phrases merely involved the mutual exchange of scriptural texts, the meaning of "mutual exchange" was not fully established. To establish this meaning of mutual exchange, they are contrasted with names such as the *Avataṃsaka*, which share the same name but differ in meaning.
Although the first phrase cites the four great śrāvakas, it generally refers to arhats, the meaning, and the three weeks.
As for the ordinary beings cited in the second phrase, the principle applies to both the beginning and the end.
Regarding the fact that the meaning of the subsequent phrase encompasses both the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* teachings, it differs from the preceding first phrase.

As for the remaining two phrases stating "as above," this refers to the explanation of the Śākyamuni chapter in the preceding verses; therein, the four "ones" at the end of the verse and the four phrases in the analytical section are largely identical to the present text, yet there are slight differences, which is why they are explained again here.
The first sentence states that this occurred during the period of the Tripiṭaka, without mentioning the end of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and so forth.
The second sentence merely speaks of "all ordinary beings within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*" and does not mention persons from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Although their wording differs, their essential meaning is the same.
When it says, "The remaining two are as above," this refers to the third and fourth lines.

That text states that when obstacles are removed, the capacity [for awakening] is immediately triggered; this is like those who attained the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle in the *Anantaryārtha-sūtra* hearing the Great [Vehicle] while still on their seats.

When hindrances have not yet been removed and the capacity has not yet been awakened, as in the case of the five thousand who rose and departed, only those in the fourth category are not among the people of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
From "If [one possesses] great capacity" onwards, the text further reiterates the preceding passage through a rearrangement of its components.

Regarding the phrase "if [there are] great-capacity [beings]" and so forth: as previously cited from the text of the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paryāya*), although the textual sequence of that chapter has its own internal order, it does not mean that the great-capacity beings first give rise to their aspiration and only later have their obstacles removed.
Regarding the phrase "if the prior obstructions have been removed," this refers to the passage cited above beginning with "Now, in the analogy... and continuing below.

As for "the four truths converging in the vision of the truths," there is also an analogy of the crossroads in the *Āgama* sūtras concerning the exhaustion of afflictions beneath the realization of the four truths.

Next, the meaning of "seeking the vehicle" is clarified. Regarding the phrase "formulating ten difficulties," this refers to ancient scholars who established these objections, refusing to admit that Bodhisattvas have the sense of seeking a vehicle, or that the two [vehicles] are merged into one.
That it has been revived in recent times—what is there to find strange in that?
Therefore, I shall now provide a refutation so that those who seek to understand may assemble.
First, I will present their arguments; second, I will refute them.

The first two [cases] are visible; regarding the third, it is said that those being transformed are ordinary beings who have not yet emerged from the triple world, and thus they should not possess a cord.
The capacity to transform resides in the thirty-third mind-moment; one cannot further claim that a cord exists at this stage.
If one enters the fruit of Buddhahood, the fruit of Buddhahood is non-dual; from whom, then, would a Buddha seek anything?

Fourth, it clarifies that although the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) have been severed first, the residual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and ignorance remain; logically, there is no reason to seek them. When these are completely severed and one attains Buddhahood, the Buddha has nothing further to seek.
The fifth [section] cites the current scriptural passage to prove that it concerns the Bodhisattva.

Regarding the sixth, which says "from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*," etc., since in ancient times the *Prajñā* was considered to precede the *Vaipulya*, it is said to be "from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* onwards."
First, the objection is raised by citing the statement, "All that prior to the *Lotus Sūtra* was expedient means," which establishes the premise;
the section beginning with "Entrusting the Poor Son" sets forth the challenge.
Since the realization of the two vehicles is entirely the Dharma of a bodhisattva, if what was entrusted were merely expedient wealth, why would it be said, "All this is my own possession"?
"If the entrusted wealth" refers to a further inquiry.

If the wealth entrusted were already real, then since the Bodhisattva had previously obtained this wealth and it was already established as real, why would he seek its reality again at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?

Regarding the seventh meaning, the "Expedient Means" chapter states that "it is not something that can be known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Therefore, the Lesser Vehicle is termed "expedient means," and for this reason, it must be sought.

Regarding "the Buddha-sons of the Mahāyāna," the verse says: "The Buddha-sons, having practiced the Way, shall become Buddhas in future ages. Becoming a Buddha is the reality; as it is reality, there is no need to seek it.
The lower three are visible [in the text].
What has been calculated by scholars of both ancient and modern times does not exceed these ten.
Regarding the subsequent refutation, the phrase "I have privately refuted them in terms of both the general and the specific" means that it is a private refutation.
“Bó” (駁) refers to a mottled or variegated appearance, a state of impurity; it also implies mixture.
To “shatter” them as if they were mottled is the correct interpretation, whereas [interpreting them as] pure is not.
What is called “comprehensive” (總) means that, generally establishing the Bodhisattvas’ sense of seeking a vehicle, all ten meanings are thereby shattered.

Regarding the passage from "Seeking is requesting" to "is called seeking," it cites the preceding three types of action, all of which contain the term "seeking" (*paryeṣaṇā*); this is presented through the triad of the Dharma, the analogy, and the application.
Regarding "the intention of the Dharma": those of the three vehicles have not yet fully realized their dwelling nor perfected their practice; they must all come to this sutra to seek [its meaning].
The three phrases in the analogy correspond, in sequence, to the three dharmas.

In the section "The General Dwelling," the first part clarifies the intent of the request; the meaning of the request encompasses three aspects, and the supporting texts are cited in full to present the matter from beginning to end.

Since permission is granted because of the request, and the gift is given because of the permission, and since there are textual records of such granting and giving, how could it be that there was no request?
In the initial section clarifying the request, since Maitreya was first among those who requested [the teaching], how could the granting of permission pertain solely to Śāriputra?

Furthermore, as Śāriputra’s universal request benefits both himself and others, he says, "I pray you, for the sake of the fourfold assembly. How could these fourfold assemblies consist of only the two vehicles?
Since the Buddha permitted that this was not intended for a limited group alone, he spoke generally of "I shall preach for you" and so forth; this can be seen in the scriptural text.
Thus, we know that the three cycles of teaching apply universally to all three vehicles.
"The teaching of the Dharma concluded, Śāriputra rejoiced" refers to the beginning of the second fascicle.

"The teaching by way of parables concluded, Kāśyapa rejoiced" is as stated at the beginning of the *Adhimukty-adhikāra*: "Upon hearing the World-Honored One bestow a prediction upon Śāriputra, he gave rise to a heart of rare wonder and leaped for joy."

Regarding the phrase "Kulūna rejoiced at the conclusion of his past lives," it is as stated at the beginning of the *Pañcaśata-vyākaraṇa*: "Furthermore, hearing the account of the causes and conditions of his past lives, his mind became pure and he leaped with joy."

Next, regarding "Specific Refutations": first, the refutation of the first point concerning the statement that "according to the Tripiṭaka Master, Bodhisattvas do not sever the afflictions. Previously it was stated that because Bodhisattvas have not yet reached the state of certainty (*niyāma*), they do not reach the fruit of certainty together with the Two Vehicles due to their failure to sever the afflictions; thus, they are not [the ones] being sought. Since it is only within the Tripiṭaka that it is taught that Bodhisattvas do not sever [the afflictions], it is therefore judged and stated as "equal to" (*sama*).

Regarding the statement, "According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there are four propositions," this means that, following the present sutra, one must employ a fourfold categorization to fully encompass all types of practitioners (*yogins*). If these four propositions were absent, there would be a fear that people might believe the arousal of the spiritual capacity (*gotra*) occurs only for those who are free from obstructions; therefore, the second proposition refers to the bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka.
If one speaks only of the two vehicles, when have the obstacles of the two vehicles ever been eliminated?

To pursue the essential point, I shall first list the two phrases regarding "capacity" (*jī*) and "arousing" (*fā*) to refute the old [interpretation] without further inquiry. If there is no inquiry, how can there be an arousing of capacity?
Nevertheless, there are cases where the capacity [of the faculties] does not move yet obstructions are nonetheless removed; this is the third phrase.

"Not yet having moved" refers for now to the period prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; once that sūtra is reached, with the exception of the five thousand [who left], there are none who do not have their capacities move.
Regarding the refutation of the second point, that teacher’s intention is as follows:

"The seeking [of the Lesser Vehicle] exists only in the Lesser Vehicle; none of the Mahāyāna sūtras state that bodhisattvas seek the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle. How, then, could the bodhisattvas in this present sūtra possibly seek the Lesser Vehicle?"

Therefore, the present refutation asks: "Since entering *nirvāṇa* is the same for all, how can it be that some do not seek [the ultimate]? This is refuted by means of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*). You claim that Bodhisattvas do not seek the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle;

however, since those who attain the principle through the three vehicles are identical, they are all equally dismissed as being merely provisional (*upāya*). If one wishes to further seek the true principle, one must seek it together with them. If even those of the Shared Teaching must seek it, how much more so those of the Tripitaka?
Regarding the refutation of the third position, that text states:

"From the time of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and one hundred *kalpas* until reaching the stage of the 'one destined for Buddhahood' (*upapadya-bodhisattva*), they are still ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) according to the principle of having no [definitive] search.
This is an excessive depreciation; how could it be that during the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and one hundred *kalpas*, they are consistently identical to ordinary beings?

The text remains unrefuted; however, because its ability to transform the thirty-three types of mental activity has not yet been fully exhausted, one should not seek [further]. Upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, there is again no sense of seeking a vehicle; rather, it is simply judged in general terms as belonging to the Tripiṭaka.

Therefore, it may be acceptable that one is still called a bodhisattva during the thirty-two moments of mind beneath the Bodhi tree, as the duration is so brief that the full realization of the meaning cannot yet be accomplished;
however, to say that the contemplation is not yet complete would be incorrect.

Therefore, using ordinary people with delusions of views as an analogy: if such delusional obstructions remain entirely intact yet the great-capacity [bodhisattvas] still manifest [realization], how much more so for those at the thirty-third mind?

It is said that the Buddha does not seek logical consistency; thus, they do not even know that the cause reaches the fruit. By the time of the thirty-third mind, there is certainly no longer any practice of realization; one merely halts midway through this Buddha’s true path, which consists of reaching the fruit after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* by severing only the delusions of views and cultivation—thereby becoming identical to an Arhat. As it is said, "There are six types of Arhats in the world," so how could these Arhats not request a vehicle?

It is solely because they do not understand the provisional (upāya) that they are first challenged; since their teaching is provisional, there are obstacles both in its progression and its regression.

Within the refutation of the fourth point, it likewise first restates the objection, saying: "The Bodhisattva has not yet severed the residual habits (vāsanā)" up to "until they are completely exhausted," and so forth. This uses the third passage as an example: if, according to the preceding third passage, the Bodhisattva proceeds to sever the residual habits and ignorance, then logically they would become a Buddha, and the meaning of "seeking" (or "requesting") would not be established.

The passage beginning with "These three vehicles" correctly judges them as belonging to the Shared [Teaching]. Since this teaching is not yet ultimate, bodhisattvas must still seek it; next, the state of being bound by all fetters is used as an illustration.
As for refuting the fifth point: that position holds that among the three vehicles, the bodhisattva is the only one [to attain Buddhahood].

Next, the section "The Confrontation" below refutes this: even if one grants that the bodhisattvas' subduing and severing [of afflictions] differ from those of the two vehicles, they are still called "the only one" in relation to the two vehicles. One should know that the term "the only one" is applied generally in relation to the two [vehicles] and is not restricted; it refers to the fact that outside of those two which serve as the point of reference, there is only one. Thus, they do not realize that within each of the four teachings, the bodhisattvas of that respective teaching are also called "the only one. Therefore, although there are three instances of "the only one," they must still seek the carriage.

One should know that the first three [teachings] involve duality and are merely "one" in relation to that duality; only the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is the "one" that is absolute and beyond dependence (*juedai*). This is because, just as there are still three other teachings outside the "one" of the Tripitaka Teaching (Sanzang), the same can be understood regarding the Shared and Distinct Teachings.
“Night-light” refers to the bright moon-pearl.
Regarding the “breaking of the sixth consciousness,” he means that from the *Prajñāpāramitā* up to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there is a single, uniform reality.

The passage beginning with “You have not... rebukes him by means of the common and the uncommon; this text on the common and uncommon originates from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. One might allow that the uncommon [truth] need not be sought for a bodhisattva, as they already possess the perfect [teaching].
Furthermore, there are both exclusive and shared [teachings]; if even the exclusive ones must be sought, how much more so the shared ones for a bodhisattva?
Thus, you do not understand that the wealth entrusted to you includes both the shared and the exclusive, yet you unilaterally claim that it is truly not to be sought.

Furthermore, if it is said that within the Prajñāpāramitā, the Bodhisattva does not truly seek [anything], yet now one objects to this by asking: since the Two Vehicles have been entrusted with the truth therein, they are identical to the Bodhisattva; why then would they need to seek further?
Moreover, you yourself have stated that everything from [the teachings] up to the *Lotus Sūtra* is entirely true; this is because you do not understand the differences between the three flavors.

Having concluded the citation of the objection within the refutation of the seventh [point], the text next cites a passage from the "Original Gate" (*Honmon*) to refute it. Since, according to that text of the "Original Gate," both the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as self and others, are all expedient means (*upāya*), how much more so must the partial [teachings] be expedient when compared to the Perfect [teaching] of that original text?

Now, the three teachings within the迹 (traces) are all skillful means; how much more so when the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter states, "The Buddha, by the power of expedient means, reveals the teachings of the three vehicles. When could it ever be said that he revealed only the two vehicles?
Because these three are simultaneous expedients, they are collectively sought.

Regarding the refutation of the eighth [position], one first sets forth the objection; next, from "Do you not hear... onwards, it is refuted. Furthermore, one should additionally cite the introductory passages from the ten points at the beginning of the previous three cycles.
The refutation of the ninth [point] has already been established as before.
Regarding the refutation of the tenth, which states "it is still the same meaning as before," it does not go beyond the Three Piṭakas; thus, its refutation is also as before.

Most people who understand the meaning of the teachings do not accept the words of the four teachings; here, we shall merely refute them by stating that the four stages and the shared positions of the three vehicles are different from those of the Bodhisattvas in the *Avataṃsaka*.

"If you do not accept them, please take back the *Vibhāṣā*, the *Abhidharmakośa*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* to India. Regarding the phrase "having one's own practice of cessation" and so forth:

because there is a distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles, in the Lesser Vehicle one seeks cessation; in the case of the Bodhisattva, one seeks it because the provisional teachings have not yet ceased.

Furthermore, from "Moreover, the Bodhisattva" onwards, the argument is refuted through further reasoning. "Seeking" (*suo*) is a synonym for requesting; how could one obtain something without seeking it?
Regarding the phrase "returning to its deceptive entanglements," "deceptive" (*gui*) means fraudulent.
"Accumulation" (*lei*) means layering or piling up.

Most of the ten meanings involve deception, accumulation, and concealment of the *āgama* (Tripitaka) and *śrāvaka* (Shared) teachings; thus, the first, third, ninth, and tenth are entirely of the Tripitaka school. The fourth, fifth, and sixth are broadly attached to the Shared Teaching. The remaining three meanings contain elements of both the Tripitaka and the Shared teachings. This is because, according to the *Ratnavyūha-sūtra*, their stages and practices still belong to provisional application (*upāya*), as there is no distinction between the initial resolve and the two [subsequent] stages;
if these were truly real, would they not be identical to the practices and vows of Samantabhadra in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*?

Is this not so? Thus, even within our own school (*ekācārya*), when establishing a distinct doctrine, one must still seek clarification; how much more so for the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Vaipulya* (Shared) teachings!

Because those [schools] establish that Bodhisattvas do not sever [afflictions], and because their severance of delusions is not exhaustive, there is no need to seek [clarification]. However, since the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) sever delusions, it is necessary to seek it. This implies that even a Bodhisattva who is entirely confused regarding the severance of delusions must seek the vehicle; how much more so for one whose hindrances have not yet been removed and whose great capacity has been activated?
The passage beginning with "Now, when" is divided below into four propositions: severance and non-severance, seeking and non-seeking; how much more so for the sixteen propositions in their entirety.

Based on the five periods, the initial allowance for the ancients causes them to fall into one proposition; if they reach the sixteen propositions, it causes that which was without seeking to become seeking, entirely causing them to fall into a state where no "non-being" proposition can be attained.
Within this, four propositions are first set forth.
Question:
How does the first proposition differ from that of the ancient masters regarding the Bodhisattva who does not seek?
Answer:
There is now a distinct intention here, as it is determined to belong within the Tripitaka.
That [text] states that all bodhisattvas do not seek because they have not severed [afflictions], or because they have severed them but not yet exhausted them; for this reason, they do not seek.
Furthermore, I have cited sutras and treatises to form a general compendium because they were unaware of the specific meanings of the Separate (Bie) and Perfect (Yuan) teachings.
Had they known them from the outset, what would not have been established?

Therefore, at the beginning, I shall first distinguish them into four propositions to correspond with the Four Teachings, followed by a progression through the Five Flavors. Thus, within the first proposition, when compared to the latter three, the names are the same as those of the ancient masters, yet their underlying intent is eternally different; for the time being, these paired propositions are established merely as fundamental designations without further inquiry.

Because the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka maintain continuity from beginning to end, even when they are rebuked, there is nothing further to be sought; yet, although this is generally the case, it does not yet exhaust the full principle, which is why it is further expanded into sixteen propositions.
Furthermore, regarding the second phrase of the fundamental verses as referring to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao): since the three vehicles all sever [delusions], they all seek the carriage.

As for the third phrase, it is called "not severed" with reference to the stage before the ignorance of the ground (mūlamoha) is destroyed; therefore, there is a need to seek. Once one has ascended to the stages (bhūmi), this ignorance is severed and thus there is no seeking. This view is eternally distinct from all teachers of the past and present; moreover, in the fourth phrase, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu)—what further could be severed or sought?

Therefore, only the fourth phrase is called "not seeking"; although one may not seek at the outset within the first three phrases, in the end one must inevitably seek, and thus all three phrases are collectively termed "seeking."
Those with sharp faculties sought it first; those with dull faculties seek it now. Because it must be opened, it must necessarily be sought.
Even in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), one should not even speak of "not seeking," so how could there be any seeking at all?
Therefore, this does not accord with the ten meanings established by the ancients.
Next, I shall further explain the quantity of teachings according to their respective flavors by following the same principle.

Thus, while it is permissible for Bodhisattvas of the three prior teachings to seek [the Lotus Sūtra], the two vehicles of the two [final] teachings differ in terms of temporal sequence and manifest versus esoteric revelation; this is precisely why the analogy of the five flavors is so appropriate.
Regarding the phrase "the grand framework and great system," four propositions are established to correspond to the five flavors; this is because they have not yet been subdivided.
As for the phrase "each and every proposition," it is as in the aforementioned four propositions.

Regarding "each and every intent" (*yiyi*): if one directly addresses the phrases, they are simply the fourfold teaching phrases; yet because these are further distinguished from the four, the phrases are also called "intent. "Intent" refers precisely to the phrases within the teachings, as in the expression "the two intents of the flavor of milk," and so forth.
Thus we know that the removal of hindrances is simply the severance of delusions, and when the spiritual capacity is activated, it is logically appropriate to seek the vehicle.

According to this middle phrase, if one takes the first of the four fundamental phrases as the primary basis, one should first distinguish four cases based on the hindrances not being removed and the capacity not being activated: (1) neither removed nor activated; (2) already removed but not yet activated; (3) both removed and not removed but not yet activated; and (4) neither removed nor not removed but not yet activated. Since "not yet activated" is not the central theme, it is not employed here.

The initial passage first correlates "removing" (*chú*) and so forth with "movement" (*dòng*). This appears to be derived from the second line of the fundamental [text], as it states that each line is further divided into four. Thus, these four lines are simply enumerated across the various teachings; in this way, each of the four teachings takes "removing" and so forth in contrast to "movement" as its thematic line to clarify the "seeking of the carriage. Since the core principle lies in "movement," every teaching employs the correlation of "removing" and so forth with "movement. Therefore, the text merely lists the four lines as a formal model, yet proceeds to apply these lines across the five flavors (*wèi*) to distinguish them, thereby making known that within the various capacities of the [first] four flavors, they are not yet uniform, and thus there are differences between the respective teaching and the subsequent teaching.

According to the intent of the present sutra, although there are various teachings regarding whether hindrances are removed or not, the arousal of the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) must pertain exclusively to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Question: Regarding the first three teachings, it is evident that when their respective teachings are discussed in terms of the arousal [of the capacity], they correspond to the removal or non-removal of hindrances within those same respective teachings. However, this is not so for the Perfect Teaching. Why? Because the Perfect Teaching encompasses all capacities; therefore, while the arousal of the capacity may be categorized according to the specific teaching, the removal of hindrances is necessarily based on the Perfect Teaching itself. Furthermore, the Perfect Teaching is the ultimate truth; thus, even if one speaks of the removal of hindrances according to the specific teaching, it is in fact the Perfect Teaching that effects such removal. This is because the Perfect Teaching is the root of all teachings. For example, when the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of the removal of hindrances, it does so from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching. Therefore, although the arousal of the capacity may be categorized according to the specific teaching, the removal of hindrances is necessarily based on the Perfect Teaching. Consequently, the Perfect Teaching is the ultimate truth.
